cards.title: CQRS Overview
cards.teaser: Command-Query Responsibility Segregation splits a service into two distinct models: one for writes and one for reads. Greg Young coined the term in 2010, extending Bertrand Meyer's Command-Query Separation principle to the architectural level.

runs.text: Command-Query Responsibility Segregation — CQRS — is an architectural pattern that insists a single data model cannot serve both write operations and read operations well. Greg Young formalized the term around 2010, building on Bertrand Meyer's earlier Command-Query Separation (CQS) principle, which stated that a method should either change state (a command) or return data (a query), but never both.
CQRS elevates that idea from individual methods to whole subsystems. The result is two logically (and often physically) separate models:

items.text: Write model (command side)
— accepts commands, enforces business rules, and persists authoritative state.
Read model (query side)
— serves queries from a separately maintained, query-optimized store.

runs.text: Martin Fowler notes that CQRS is frequently misunderstood as a top-level architecture for an entire system. In practice it is a pattern applied selectively to specific bounded contexts or services — those where the read and write workloads are genuinely asymmetric. Applied everywhere, it becomes unnecessary complexity.

Greg Young: "CQRS is simply the creation of two objects where there was previously only one. The separation occurs based upon whether the methods are a command or a query." The key word is 'simply' — CQRS itself is not complex. The complexity it introduces comes from managing two models, not from the pattern itself.

Instead of one model that handles both saving data and fetching it, CQRS uses two separate models: one optimized for accepting commands that change state, and another optimized for answering queries. The two models stay in sync asynchronously.

cards.title: The Motivation — Read and Write Workloads Have Different Shapes
cards.teaser: Writes need correctness: validation, invariant checking, and transactional consistency. Reads need performance: joins across many entities, aggregated views, and sub-millisecond response. One normalized relational schema cannot excel at both simultaneously.

runs.text: In a traditional architecture, the same database schema serves all operations. An order table must be normalized enough that inserts, updates, and deletes remain consistent — and yet flat enough that a product catalog page can render quickly without eight-table joins.
These two goals pull in opposite directions:

items.text: Write workloads

are typically low-throughput, transaction-bound operations. A customer places one order. The system must validate payment, check inventory, and record the event atomically. Correctness matters more than raw speed.
Read workloads

are typically high-throughput, complex aggregations. Every page load, dashboard refresh, or mobile feed triggers multiple queries across many entity types. Speed matters more than strict consistency at that millisecond.

runs.text: The asymmetry compounds in microservices. A single service may own only a slice of the data. A query that spans orders, customers, products, and shipping lives across four services. Joining across service boundaries via API calls is slow and fragile. CQRS resolves this by allowing each service to maintain a pre-joined, denormalized read model that answers cross-service queries directly.

A useful rule of thumb: if a system's read-to-write ratio exceeds 10:1 and the read queries require joining more than two or three tables, CQRS is worth considering. Below that threshold, a well-indexed relational schema with read replicas will likely suffice.

Writes need rules; reads need speed. A single normalized schema is a compromise between the two. CQRS stops compromising: it gives writes the schema they need for correctness and reads the schema they need for performance.

cards.title: The Architecture Contrast
cards.teaser: A diagram makes the split concrete. In a unified architecture, commands and queries share the same model. In CQRS, they flow to entirely separate models, synchronized asynchronously.

runs.text: Unified (traditional) architecture:

explanation.text:
Client
  |
  |--- Command (PlaceOrder) ---->
  |                              |
  |<-- Query  (GetOrderStatus) --+
                                 |
                          [Service Layer]
                                 |
                    [Single Normalized DB Model]
                    (orders, items, customers...)

runs.text: CQRS architecture:

explanation.text:
Client
  |
  |--- Command (PlaceOrder) ---------> [Command Handler]
  |                                         |
  |                                  [Write Model / DB]
  |                                    (normalized,
  |                                     transactional)
  |                                         |
  |                                   [Event / Change]
  |                                         |
  |                                   [Projection]
  |                                         |
  |                                  [Read Model / DB]
  |                                  (denormalized,
  |                                   query-optimized)
  |                                         |
  |<-- Query (GetOrderSummary) ----------- [Query Handler]

runs.text: The key differences visible in the diagram:

items.text: Commands and queries never touch the same model.
The read model is derived from the write model via a projection step, not via direct writes.
The two models can use entirely different storage technologies (relational for writes, document or search index for reads).

runs.text: In a unified architecture everything flows through one model. In CQRS the write path and the read path are completely separate tracks, with a one-way synchronization step deriving the read model from what the write model produces.

cards.title: Write Model (Command Side)
cards.teaser: The write model owns the truth. It enforces all business invariants, validates commands, maintains transactional consistency, and records state changes. It is deliberately kept lean — it does not serve queries.

runs.text: The command side handles all state-changing operations: placing an order, cancelling a shipment, updating a customer address. Its primary responsibilities are:

items.text: Validation
— reject commands that violate business rules (e.g., an order cannot be placed if the customer's account is suspended).
Invariant enforcement
— ensure aggregate consistency. An order aggregate ensures that no line item is added after the order is confirmed.
Persistence
— write authoritative state atomically. This is the source of truth.
Change publication
— emit an event or notification that the read model can consume to stay in sync.

runs.text: Critically, the write model is
not

optimized for queries. Its schema is normalized for correctness, not for read performance. In an order management system, the write model stores orders and line items in separate tables with full referential integrity — even though a typical query needs them joined. That join is the read model's problem.

Because the write model is not queried directly by clients, it can evolve its internal schema without breaking the query API. The only contract the write model has with the outside world is the events or change notifications it emits.

In domain-driven design terms, the command side aligns naturally with aggregates: each command targets one aggregate root, the aggregate enforces invariants, and the transaction boundary matches the aggregate boundary. CQRS and DDD aggregate design are a natural pairing.

The write model is the authority on what is true. It validates every change, enforces every rule, and records authoritative state. It never serves queries — it just writes, then signals that something changed.

cards.title: Read Model (Query Side)
cards.teaser: The read model is purpose-built for queries. It is denormalized, materialized, and optimized around the shapes of queries it must answer — not around the rules of the domain it represents.

runs.text: The query side stores data in whatever shape makes queries fast and simple. For an order management system, several distinct read models might coexist:

items.text: Order summary view
— a flat document per order containing order ID, customer name, total, status, and item count. No joins required. Served from a document store.
Customer order history
— a list of abbreviated order records indexed by customer ID. Pre-sorted by date descending. Served from a key-value store.
Fulfillment dashboard
— orders grouped by status and warehouse, refreshed every 30 seconds. Served from a materialized view in a search index.

runs.text: The read model has two defining characteristics:

items.text: Derived, not owned.
The read model never receives direct writes from clients. All its data is derived from the write model via projections. It can be thrown away and rebuilt from scratch at any time.
Eventually consistent.
The read model reflects the write model as of some recent point in time, not necessarily right now. A newly placed order may not appear in the order history query for a few hundred milliseconds.

runs.text: Because the read model is disposable and derived, it carries no risk of data loss. If the projection logic changes, you rebuild the read model from the source of truth (the write model or its event log). This makes schema evolution on the read side far less dangerous than on a unified model.

The read model is a cache shaped exactly like your queries. It holds no authoritative data of its own — it is derived from the write model and can be rebuilt whenever needed. Queries hit this cache, not the write model.

cards.title: Projections
cards.teaser: A projection is the code that derives the read model from write-side changes. It listens to events or change notifications, computes the new read model state, and writes it to the query store. It is the bridge between the two models.

runs.text: In the CQRS data flow, a projection is a consumer that:

items.text: 1. Receives
an event or change notification from the write side (e.g., OrderPlaced, OrderShipped).
2. Transforms
the event data into the shape required by the read model.
3. Writes
the result into the query store (update a document, upsert a row, increment a counter).

runs.text: In the order management example, an OrderPlaced event triggers the order-summary projection to create a new document in the document store. An OrderShipped event triggers the same projection to update the status field of that document. The fulfillment-dashboard projection maintains separate counters per status per warehouse.
Projections have important properties:

items.text: Idempotency.
A projection must be able to process the same event twice without corrupting the read model. Use at-least-once delivery with idempotent writes (e.g., upsert by event ID).
Replayability.
If the read model is deleted or corrupted, replay the event log from the beginning to rebuild it. This requires the event log to be durable and ordered.
Independence.
Each read model has its own projection. Adding a new query shape means adding a new projection — not modifying the write model.

runs.text: Projections that are not idempotent are a production hazard. Message brokers typically guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. Any projection that cannot safely process a duplicate event will corrupt the read model silently.

A projection listens to events from the write side and uses them to update the read model. It is the bridge that keeps the two models in sync. If you replay all the events, you can rebuild the read model from scratch.

cards.title: Eventual Consistency Between Models
cards.teaser: The read model trails the write model by design. After a command succeeds, a client querying the read model may not yet see the change. This asynchrony is not a bug — it is the mechanism that makes independent scaling possible.

runs.text: When a user places an order, the system:

items.text: Writes the order to the write model (transactional, immediately consistent).
Emits an OrderPlaced event to a message broker.
The projection consumes the event and updates the read model — some milliseconds later.

runs.text: If the client immediately queries the order history, step 3 may not have completed. The read model returns stale data. This is eventual consistency: the system guarantees that the read model
will
reflect the write, just not synchronously.
Handling eventual consistency in the UI:

items.text: Optimistic UI updates.
After a command succeeds, show the expected new state in the UI immediately without waiting for a query to confirm it. Roll back if a subsequent query reveals failure.
Polling or server-sent events.
The client polls the read model until it reflects the command, or the server pushes a notification when the projection has caught up.
Version tokens.

The command response returns a version number. The query request includes that version as a minimum consistency token, and the query handler waits until the read model has caught up to that version before responding.

runs.text: Eventual consistency is only acceptable if the UI and the business process can tolerate it. Financial account balances, inventory availability, and seat reservation are examples where strong consistency is required — CQRS with its inherent lag is a poor fit for those writes.

After you write something, the read model catches up a moment later. During that gap, queries return slightly stale data. That lag is the price of having separate, independently scalable models — and it is usually acceptable if the UI is designed with it in mind.

cards.title: CQRS Without Event Sourcing
cards.teaser: CQRS does not require event sourcing. The simpler form uses a standard database for writes, emits change notifications via database triggers or outbox patterns, and maintains a separate read store. This is often the right starting point.

runs.text: The relationship between CQRS and event sourcing (ES) is commonly misunderstood. Many developers assume CQRS requires ES. It does not. They are independent patterns that compose well but can be used separately.
CQRS without event sourcing:

items.text: Write model
— a standard relational database. Commands update rows and tables via CRUD operations. No event log is maintained.
Change notification
— the write model publishes domain events after each successful write, using the Transactional Outbox pattern to guarantee at-least-once delivery without distributed transactions.
Read model
— a separate store (e.g., a Redis cache, a read replica, a document DB) kept in sync by a projection that consumes those events.

runs.text: This form is simpler to adopt and carry lower operational cost. The trade-off: since there is no persistent event log, rebuilding the read model from scratch requires either snapshotting the write model's current state or running a data migration. You lose the ability to replay history.
CQRS without ES is the right choice when:

items.text: The team is unfamiliar with event sourcing and wants to adopt CQRS incrementally.
Historical replay of all events is not required for business or audit reasons.
The write model's schema is stable and unlikely to require historical recomputation.

runs.text: You can do CQRS with a plain relational database for writes. Use the Outbox pattern to publish change events, and let a projection update a separate read store. No event log required — but without one, you cannot replay history.

cards.title: CQRS With Event Sourcing
cards.teaser: Event sourcing is a natural write model for CQRS. Instead of storing current state, it stores the full sequence of events that produced that state. Projections replay those events to build any read model, and new projections can be added at any time.

runs.text: When the write model uses event sourcing, it stores an append-only log of domain events — OrderPlaced, PaymentConfirmed, OrderShipped — rather than the current state of the order. To reconstruct an order's current state, the aggregate replays its events in sequence.
This makes CQRS projections extremely powerful:

items.text: Replayability
— the event log is the source of truth. Any read model can be deleted and rebuilt by replaying all events from the beginning. New projections can be bootstrapped against historical data instantly.
Time travel
— project events up to any point in time to reconstruct historical state. Useful for audits, debugging, and retroactive analytics.
Multiple consistent projections
— the same event stream drives many projections independently. Each read model is derived from the same authoritative history.

runs.text: The CQRS + ES combination does carry additional complexity:

items.text: Event schema evolution
— old events must remain processable by new projection code. Versioning strategies (upcasting, event versioning) must be planned from the start.
Snapshot management
— replaying thousands of events per aggregate on every write is slow. Periodic snapshots of aggregate state are required for long-lived aggregates.
Operational overhead
— an event store infrastructure (EventStoreDB, Kafka, or a custom table) adds operational cost.

runs.text: Greg Young: event sourcing is not a caching strategy or an optimization — it is a fundamentally different way of modeling state. The event log is the database. Current state is a derived view. This mental model shift is the steepest part of the adoption curve.

When you pair CQRS with event sourcing, the write side stores a log of everything that ever happened. Projections replay that log to build query-optimized views. You can add a new query shape later and replay the entire history to populate it immediately.

cards.title: Multiple Read Models
cards.teaser: A single write model can feed many read models simultaneously. Each read model is shaped for a specific query or consumer. This is CQRS's answer to the problem of one schema that must serve a dozen different query patterns.

runs.text: Consider the order management domain. The OrderPlaced, OrderShipped, and OrderCancelled events stream from the write model into multiple independent projections, each producing a different read model:

items.text: Customer portal projection
— stores a flat order-summary document per order. Fields: order ID, date, status, total, item count. Indexed by customer ID. Technology: document store.
Warehouse fulfillment projection
— stores open orders grouped by warehouse and product SKU. Recalculated on every inventory-relevant event. Technology: relational view with spatial index.
Analytics projection
— appends one row per order event to a time-series table. Powers revenue-over-time and funnel analysis dashboards. Technology: columnar data warehouse.
Search projection
— indexes order metadata and customer name for full-text search by the support team. Technology: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch.

runs.text: Each projection is independent:

items.text: A failure in the analytics projection does not affect the customer portal.
Each projection can lag at its own rate — the search index might be seconds behind; the analytics warehouse might be minutes behind.
Adding a new consumer means adding a new projection, not modifying the write model.

runs.text: Martin Fowler calls this the 'reporting database' pattern when applied to the analytics use case — a separate store optimized for reporting queries, fed from the operational system. CQRS generalizes this to all query patterns, not just reporting.
One write model, many read models. Each read model is shaped for exactly the queries it must answer. Adding a new query shape means adding a new projection — the write model does not change.

cards.title: Synchronizing Read Models
cards.teaser: Keeping read models current requires a reliable pipeline from write-side changes to projection handlers. The key mechanisms are the Transactional Outbox pattern, message brokers, and careful handling of ordering, idempotency, and lag monitoring.

runs.text: The synchronization pipeline has three components:

items.text: Event publishing

— how write-side changes become events visible to projections. The Transactional Outbox pattern writes events to an outbox table in the same transaction as the domain state change, then a relay process reads from the outbox and publishes to a message broker. This avoids dual-write consistency problems.
Message broker
— Kafka, RabbitMQ, or AWS EventBridge delivers events to projection consumers. The broker provides durability, ordering (within a partition), and replay capability.
Projection handler
— the consumer that processes events and writes the read model. Must be idempotent. Must checkpoint its position in the event stream to resume after crashes without re-processing from the beginning.

runs.text: Operational concerns:

items.text: Ordering
— events for the same aggregate must be processed in order. Use a partition key equal to the aggregate ID in Kafka to guarantee ordering per aggregate while allowing parallelism across aggregates.
Lag monitoring
— track consumer lag (the gap between published events and processed events). Alert when lag exceeds thresholds — a lagging projection means queries return stale data.
Dead-letter queues
— projection failures must not block the event stream indefinitely. Route poison messages to a DLQ for manual investigation while allowing healthy messages to continue.

runs.text: The write model publishes events via the Outbox pattern, a broker delivers them, and projection handlers update the read model. The tricky parts are guaranteeing ordering per aggregate, surviving handler crashes idempotently, and monitoring how far the read model has fallen behind.

cards.title: When CQRS Fits
cards.teaser: CQRS earns its complexity when read and write workloads genuinely differ in shape, scale, or consistency requirements — particularly in microservices where cross-service joins would otherwise require expensive API orchestration.

runs.text: CQRS fits well when one or more of these conditions hold:

items.text: High read/write asymmetry.

The system serves 100x more reads than writes. Scaling the write model independently of read capacity becomes important. A social feed, an e-commerce catalog, or a booking search are canonical examples.
Multiple query shapes.
Different consumers need the same data shaped differently. A customer UI, a support tool, a mobile API, and an analytics pipeline all have different access patterns on the same order data.
Cross-service query complexity.
In microservices, queries that span service boundaries are painful. A CQRS read model can pre-join data from multiple services, serving complex queries from a single denormalized store.
Audit and history requirements.
The combination of CQRS + event sourcing provides a full audit trail. Regulatory environments requiring traceability (financial services, healthcare) benefit from this.
Independent scaling.
The read model can be scaled horizontally (more replicas, more caching) without affecting the write model's consistency guarantees.

runs.text: Real-world examples where CQRS is commonly applied: order management systems, content management platforms, financial transaction histories, booking and reservation systems, and large-scale social feeds.

CQRS is worth the complexity when reads and writes need to scale differently, when you have many different query shapes on the same data, or when cross-service joins would otherwise be painful. The pattern earns its keep in systems with genuine asymmetry.

cards.title: When CQRS Is Overkill
cards.teaser: CQRS is one of the most over-applied patterns in the microservices world. Most CRUD services, internal tools, and low-traffic APIs do not benefit from it — and pay a steep complexity tax for nothing in return.

runs.text: Martin Fowler explicitly warns against applying CQRS broadly: "CQRS is a significant mental leap for all concerned, so it shouldn't be tackled unless the benefit is worth the jump." He identifies CQRS as appropriate only for specific bounded contexts, not as a default architecture style.
Signs that CQRS is overkill:

items.text: Simple CRUD.

A user management service that creates, reads, updates, and deletes user records with low traffic has symmetric read and write operations. A single well-indexed table serves all queries efficiently. Two models add complexity with no benefit.
Symmetric read/write traffic.
If reads and writes occur at roughly the same rate, the read model never becomes a bottleneck that needs separate scaling. CQRS solves a problem that does not exist.
One query shape.
If every consumer queries the data identically, maintaining a separate read model is pure overhead — the write model's schema already serves the query well.
Small teams.

The operational complexity of two models, a message broker, and projection handlers requires a team that can own each component. A two-person team maintaining a CQRS pipeline will spend more time on infrastructure than on product features.
Strong consistency requirements everywhere.
If the business cannot tolerate any read-after-write lag, the fundamental asynchrony of CQRS is incompatible with the requirement. Do not apply CQRS and then fight its eventual consistency model.

runs.text: The most common CQRS failure mode: a team adopts it for a greenfield service because 'it scales better,' without measuring whether scaling is actually the problem. The result is a complex system with two data models, a projection pipeline, and eventual consistency bugs — for an app handling 50 requests per second.

CQRS is overkill for most services. If your reads and writes are similar in volume and shape, and your queries are simple, a single well-designed model with good indexes beats two models every time. Apply CQRS only where asymmetry genuinely exists.

cards.title: CQRS in Practice — Order Management Example End to End
cards.teaser: Tracing a single order through a full CQRS system — from PlaceOrder command to multiple query projections — makes the abstract mechanics concrete and reveals where the real implementation decisions live.

runs.text: Scenario: a customer places an order in an e-commerce platform. The write model is a PostgreSQL database with an event outbox. The read models are a MongoDB document store (customer portal) and a Redis sorted set (warehouse queue). Kafka is the event broker.

items.text: Step 1 — Command
: The API receives POST /orders with line items and payment info. The command handler validates: customer exists, payment method valid, inventory available.
Step 2 — Write
: Within one transaction: insert order row, insert line-item rows, insert OrderPlaced event into the outbox table.
Step 3 — Relay
: The Debezium CDC relay reads the outbox table and publishes the OrderPlaced event to Kafka topic orders, partitioned by order ID.
Step 4 — Projection A (Customer Portal)
: A Kafka consumer reads the event and upserts a MongoDB document: { orderId, customerId, status: 'placed', total, itemCount, createdAt }. Query latency: ~100ms after commit.
Step 5 — Projection B (Warehouse Queue)
: A second Kafka consumer reads the same event and adds the order to a Redis sorted set keyed by warehouse ID, scored by urgency. Fulfillment staff see it within seconds.
Step 6 — Query

: The customer's order history page queries MongoDB by customerId. No join, no cross-service call — sub-10ms response. The customer may or may not see the new order yet, depending on projection lag. The UI uses optimistic updates to handle this gracefully.

runs.text: Key decision points revealed by this example:

items.text: The Outbox pattern, not a two-phase commit, ensures event publication reliability.
Kafka partition by order ID ensures per-order event ordering without sacrificing throughput.
Each projection uses a different storage technology suited to its query shape.
The UI is designed with eventual consistency in mind — not bolted on afterward.

runs.text: A command hits the write model, which persists state and drops an event in an outbox. Kafka picks it up and fans it out to multiple projections — each one updating a different read store shaped for its consumer. The customer UI shows the order optimistically while the projections catch up.
